d.title: Three components are fixed and one grows
d.caption: The system prompt and the tool descriptions are **a fixed cost per turn** (11.3), and the question is paid once. **So every strategy in this module is about the 86%** — which is also why 11.3's advice to keep the tool list short matters less than it sounds for a long conversation: trimming 53 tokens of tool descriptions is worth a fraction of what trimming the history is.

d.title: Forced by the third, and it should be decided because of the first
d.caption: **Cost rises from the first turn with no threshold — it is always happening. Latency rises gradually. The window is a cliff: it works, then it fails.** So **a team that waits for the context error has been paying the quadratic cost for however long it took to get there, and the error arrives at the worst moment — on the longest and most valuable conversations.** 7.3's finding sits in between, with quality degrading before the window is reached.

nodes.label: On the longest, most valuable conversations
nodes.sub: the worst moment to find out

d.title: The budget is a fixed number of tokens, reached by subtraction
d.caption: **The reserve is 7.3's point: a budget without it fails at generation time** — the prompt fits and there is no room left to answer. And note what the last rows say about this corpus: **the turns are small, so even 40 turns fits an 8K window, which means the cost problem bites long before the window does.** A conversation carrying pasted logs or raw tool results reverses that completely.

d.title: A turn is not a unit of anything
d.caption: **So “every 10 turns” can mean 20 tokens or 510, depending on the conversation — and it fires at the wrong time in both directions: too early on a chatty exchange of “ok” and “thanks”, where summarising costs more than it saves, and too late on one with pasted logs, where ten turns has already exceeded the budget.** It is a proxy for the thing that matters, measured in a unit that varies by 25×.

d.title: A trigger at 100% fires when summarising is no longer possible
d.caption: **The summarisation call needs the history as input, so it needs the history to still fit — you have filled the window and the operation that would free it requires room you no longer have.** 60 to 70 percent is the practical range: it leaves space for the summarisation call **and for one more turn arriving while it runs**, which in a conversational system it will.

d.title: The trigger that matches the intent, and the hardest to measure
d.caption: The real question is not *“is the history long”* but *“is the old history still relevant”* — and **a conversation that changed topic can drop its early turns entirely, while one still on the original question cannot.** But 5.4's warning applies directly: **an embedding measures similarity, not relevance, so two turns about different aspects of the same order look dissimilar — and dropping the early ones loses the order id**, which 13.3 measures as the failure that destroys the conversation.

nodes.label: Embed the first N and the last N
So it can license dropping the order id
Hence a token count as the default
nodes.sub: a proxy, but a measurable one

d.title: Two triggers, and the thing to measure afterwards is neither of them
d.caption: A **token** trigger at 60–70% as the primary, because it tracks cost and the window directly and cannot be fooled by turn size — **plus a hard cap on turns as a backstop, because one enormous turn can exceed the budget in a single step before a percentage trigger has evaluated.** Then the measurement: **whether the summarised conversation can still answer what the full one could. A trigger that fires at the right time and a summary that destroys the subject is the worse outcome, because it is harder to notice.**

nodes.label: Primary: tokens at 60-70%
nodes.sub: cannot be fooled by turn size

nodes.label: Firing late is the better failure

d.title: All five facts are in the first human turn
d.caption: Which is where real conversations put them — **the order id, the amount, the card, the date and the reason all arrive before anything else has happened.** That single property is what makes the next two sections come out the way they do: a strategy that keeps the **end** of a 19-message conversation keeps none of this, and nothing about the token count will say so.

d.title: Every window size that saves tokens keeps none of the facts
d.caption: **This is not a tuning problem: there is no window size that both saves tokens and keeps the first turn, because those are the same thing** — and no amount of adjusting it finds the order id. So the question the windowed conversation can no longer answer is *“which order are we talking about”*, **which is the entire subject of the conversation. The token count meanwhile looks excellent.**

d.title: Twenty-six tokens is the difference between one fact and five
d.caption: **These are not two strategies — they are one strategy with two prompts.** Which is 7.8's finding in a new place: **what the summary omits is permanently unrecoverable, so the summarisation prompt decides the ceiling.** And *“summarise the conversation”* gets you the vague one, **because identifiers are not narratively interesting** — the thing you cannot reconstruct is the thing a summariser has no reason to keep.

d.title: Three mechanisms, each covering another's blind spot
d.caption: **A sliding window loses the beginning, which is where the subject of the conversation usually is. Summarisation loses whatever the summariser judged unimportant — and identifiers are exactly what it drops.** So the practical shape is all three at once: **the summary covers the window's loss of the beginning, the verbatim recent turns cover the summary's loss of detail in what is still being discussed, and the system message is fixed anyway.**

nodes.label: A detailed summary, told to keep them

d.title: Smaller than the history, and still linear
d.caption: **Summarise every 8 turns and a 200-turn conversation carries 25 summaries** — so a flat summary **postpones the problem by a constant factor rather than removing it.** Which is the precise reason to go hierarchical: not that flat summarisation is bad, but that its cost curve has the same shape as the one it replaced, just with a smaller constant in front of it.

d.title: Level 2's ceiling is level 1's output, not the conversation
d.caption: A vague level 1 produces a level 2 with **no facts at all**, and **a careful top-level prompt cannot rescue it** — so **the detail requirement has to be at level 1, and the top level merely has to not drop what arrives. Getting that order wrong produces a system where the expensive, carefully-prompted step operates on nothing.** 7.8's finding with two lossy steps instead of one: every level multiplies the ways a fact can disappear.

steps.note: even the careful path lost one

d.title: Knowably wrong against unknowably wrong
d.caption: The history becomes a corpus, so every finding from modules 5 to 7 applies — chunking, missed exact terms, *“which order”* as a vocabulary-mismatch query. **But the serious objection is the last one: a similarity search always returns k turns, even when none is relevant. Carrying the last 6 turns is wrong in a knowable way — you know exactly what you dropped. Retrieving 6 is wrong in an unknowable way, because retrieval failure looks like retrieval success.**

nodes.label: The history is now a corpus
A window drops a known set
A worse position to debug from
nodes.sub: even when it is right more often

d.title: The shape is additive, not substitutive
d.caption: **No retrieval strategy reliably surfaces “what we were just talking about” — that query has no distinguishing terms**, so the recent turns are not something retrieval can replace. **What retrieval is for is a conversation spanning weeks where the relevant earlier turn is three days old and topically specific**: a genuine retrieval problem, where carrying it is not an option.

items.label: The last N turns verbatim
items.sub: what the model is mid-sentence on

d.title: Two strategies reach an indefinite session, and only one an indefinite history
d.caption: Read the last column. **A sliding window scales to any length and loses the start, which 13.3 showed is fatal on its own. Hierarchical summarisation is roughly constant and reaches an indefinite session. Retrieval reaches an indefinite history** — a different claim, and the one that matters for a conversation resumed after a month. Which is why §05's shape uses the last three rows together rather than choosing between them.

d.title: Forty-eight percent saved, and nothing a later turn needs was lost
d.caption: **That is the case compression exists for, and it is the one strategy in this module that is not a trade. Filler, hedging and courtesy are a real fraction of an assistant's output and carry no information forward** — so removing them is a saving rather than a loss. Everything else here drops something a later turn might have wanted; this drops something no later turn can use.

d.title: The largest saving is on the destructive case
d.caption: **The reason is structural: dense, information-bearing text is exactly the text that cannot be shortened, so a high compression ratio is evidence you compressed something that was mostly filler — or that you destroyed something that was not. Which means a step tuned to maximise the saving will converge on destroying the user's statements of fact.** 6.4 found the same shape in BM25: a confident magnitude anti-correlated with usefulness.

d.title: Paid once, saved on every later turn
d.caption: **4.4 explains the ratio: JSON tokenises badly — the quoting, braces and field names are tokens carrying no information the model needs, so reformatting as `order ORD-4471, 148.50, 11 March` is not lossy, it is the same content without the syntax.** And this one is **free and exact**, which none of the other strategies are: a tool result has a known structure, so compressing it is a formatting function rather than a model call.

d.title: Three lines, and the stronger version when the facts are not enumerable
d.caption: **Mechanical, cheap, and the only thing that distinguishes a 60% saving from a 60% loss** — 13.3's check applied to a different operation. The stronger version is worth running on a handful of cases **even when you have a fact list, because the fact list only contains what you thought to write down.**

items.label: List the facts the context must preserve
items.desc: Written down before compressing, not after — a list made afterwards is a list of what survived.

items.label: Apply the compression
items.desc: Whichever of the three cases it is.

items.label: Check which facts survive
items.desc: Three lines of code, and the only check that separates a saving from a loss.

items.label: Stronger: ask both contexts the same question
items.desc: Two model calls per case, and it catches implications, tone and a constraint stated indirectly.

d.title: Four patterns, four different answers
d.caption: **ReAct needs the reasoning history, because the pattern is the model seeing what previous turns intended** — drop the `AIMessage` content and you have removed the pattern and left the loop. **A supervisor needs the workers' outputs and not their reasoning**, because outputs are what it decides on. **A swarm needs whatever the handoff passed, which is a design decision rather than an accumulation.** And plan-and-execute needs almost nothing.

nodes.label: So no single strategy fits all four
nodes.sub: the needs are different in kind

d.title: The window drops the reasoning and keeps the JSON
d.caption: A window keeping the last N messages treats `AIMessage` content as interchangeable with tool observations — **which are usually the bulky part, so the reasoning is what gets evicted.** The symptom is specific: **an agent calling the same tool with the same arguments it already used, because it is re-deriving its intent each turn from whatever survived. It looks like a reasoning failure and it is a configuration failure.** Hence the ordering: **compress tool results first**, then summarise older reasoning.

nodes.label: A window keeps the last N messages
Symptom: the same tool, same arguments

d.title: Four shapes, and the last one inverts the module
d.caption: **The supervisor's `name` field is load-bearing: a summary that loses attribution makes its next decision worse, because it decides which worker to call and can no longer tell which worker said what** — so the summarisation prompt has to preserve who produced each finding, not only the findings. **And the swarm row inverts the whole module: its risk is context loss rather than accumulation, so the strategy is about what to include rather than what to drop.**

items.label: Swarm: a task payload + the conversation id
items.sub: the risk is loss, not accumulation

d.title: One check, whatever the pattern and whatever the strategy
d.caption: 13.3 measured a sliding window destroying **all five facts** of a conversation while reporting a healthy token count — and **no amount of tuning the window size finds them.** So **the fact-survival check is the one measurement this module insists on, and it is three lines of code. Everything else here — the triggers, the hierarchy, the compression ordering — is a choice you can revisit. This is the check that tells you whether the choice was wrong.**

nodes.label: List the facts the context must keep
A token count cannot say this
Triggers and tiers are revisable
nodes.sub: this is what says they were wrong
